questions.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Flux Integral as a Surface Integral
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with normal vector $\overset{~}{n},$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨y,\,x-z,\,-2x⟩\,,\,\overset{~}{n}(x,y,z)=⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩\,,\,n=\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}\frac{\boxed{}}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\overset{~}{n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩}{\sqrt{(2x)^{2}+(-z)^{2}+(y)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,x-z,\,-2x⟩\cdot \frac{⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨y,\,x-z,\,-2x⟩\cdot ⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2xy-z(x-z)-2xy}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{{z}^{2}-xz}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{{z}^{2}-xz}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨xy,\,yz,\,xz⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-1,\,2⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨xy,\,yz,\,xz⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨xy,\,yz,\,xz⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(xy-yz+2xz) \\  & =\frac{xy-yz+2xz}{\sqrt{6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{xy-yz+2xz}{\sqrt{6}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{∬}_{S}xy-yz+2xz\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨y,\,z,\,2x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,z,\,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨y,\,2,\,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,x,\,3x+y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=-1$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 2.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=-1$ for  $0\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 2,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=-1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,x,\,3x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-(3x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-(3x+y))\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(3x+y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(-(3x+y))\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{2}[(\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+xy){|}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,]\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{2}(6+2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[6y+{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

For the surface $z=4$ for  $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$

$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨yz,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4y,\,4x,\,xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{-1}^{1}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =0\cdot 2 \\  & =0\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x-y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{6}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,6-y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+3)+(x+y)+(6-y)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{6} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,-y,\,4x+3⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x+2y+1$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{6}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+2y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,-y,\,4x+3⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨x+2y+1,\,-y,\,4x+3⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(-x-2y-1+2y+4x+3) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(3x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(3x+2)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(3x+2)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(3x+2)\cdot \sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{6}}}(3x+2)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{6}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3x+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(3x+2)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}(3x+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[y]_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+2x]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\cdot 10 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨y,\,x,\,z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=3x-y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{11}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=3x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-3,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=3x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,x,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨y,\,x,\,3x-y⟩\cdot ⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(3y-x-(3x-y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\cdot \sqrt{11}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{11}}}(4y-4x)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{11}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[4xy-2{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4y-2)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[2{y}^{2}-2y]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨-2y,\,\frac{x}{2},\,z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2y-x-5$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-1\le y\le 0.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{6}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2y-x-5$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-5,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=5.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2y-x-5$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨-2y,\,\frac{x}{2},\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨-2y,\,\frac{x}{2},\,2y-x-5⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(-2y-x+2y-x-5) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(-2x-5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(-2x-5)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+5)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+5)\cdot \sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{6}}}(2x+5)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{6}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-(2x+5)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+5)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{0}\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+5)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-[y]_{-1}^{0}\cdot [{x}^{2}+5x]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-(0+1)\cdot (1+5-0) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,z,\,y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=\frac{1}{2}x-y-1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\frac{3}{2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=\frac{1}{2}x-y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨\frac{1}{2},\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-1,\,2,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=\frac{1}{2}x-y-1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,z,\,y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-1,\,2,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,\frac{1}{2}x-y-1,\,y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,2,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-x+(x-2y-2)+2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{3})\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{3})\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{3})\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{\cancel{2}}{\cancel{3}})\cdot \frac{\cancel{3}}{\cancel{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-1\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\cdot 1 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with normal vector $\widetilde{\mathbf n},$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle x,\: 2z,\: z-y \right\rangle\!, 
\quad 
\widetilde{\mathbf{n}}(x,y,z) = \left\langle z,\: -y,\: -x \right\rangle\!,
\quad
\mathbf n = \dfrac{\widetilde{\mathbf{n}}}{\Vert \widetilde{\mathbf{n}} \Vert}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067034/assets/35bcfa2242051bed034ac3343c1a6d67f94916d4267030f726e2bd27cbbe02f1.png)

what is the missing expression?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\widetilde{\mathbf n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{(z)^{2}+(-y)^{2}+(-x)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{z}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,2z,\,z-y⟩\cdot \frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨x,\,2z,\,z-y⟩\cdot ⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{xz-2yz-x(z-y)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{xy-2yz}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{xy-2yz}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=

$$

For the surface $z=1$ for  $0\leq x\leq 1$ and $0\leq y\leq 1,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle y,\: 0,\: z\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x+2y$ for $0\leq x\leq 2$ and $0\leq y\leq 1.$ Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y|| =3.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = 0, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+2y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,0,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨y,\,0,\,2x+2y⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2y+0x+2x+2y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2x) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2}{3}x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}x\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}x\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\cancel{3}}x\cdot \cancel{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[y]_{0}^{1}\cdot [{x}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\cdot 4 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$
